content.overview: Water pH, alkalinity and EC answer different questions. pH describes current acidity/basicity, alkalinity describes acid-neutralizing capacity, and EC reflects bulk ionic conductivity rather than ion identity.

vocabulary.definition: A logarithmic measure related to hydrogen-ion activity that describes current acidity/basicity.
Acid-neutralizing capacity, commonly driven by bicarbonates and carbonates and often expressed as calcium-carbonate equivalents.
A bulk measure of ionic conductivity that responds to dissolved ions collectively but does not identify them.

sections.title: pH is not alkalinity
sections.body: Two source waters can have similar pH but different alkalinity and therefore different repeated buffering influence on the root zone.

sections.title: EC does not identify the salts
sections.body: Similar EC values can arise from different mixtures of sodium, calcium, chloride, bicarbonate or nutrients. Element-specific questions require element-specific analysis.

sections.title: Context matters
sections.body: Interpret source water with treatment history, source identity, crop use and laboratory context rather than treating a single number as a full specification.

workedExamples: A municipal source and a well may share similar pH but differ in alkalinity and mineral composition enough to behave differently over repeated irrigation.
commonMistakes: Using pH and alkalinity as synonyms.
Assuming acceptable pH/EC means all contaminants are absent.
content.practicalApplication: Compare two mock water reports and explain what each pH, alkalinity, EC and major-ion result can and cannot support.
content.summary: Water quality requires multiple measurements because no single value captures chemistry, buffering and contaminant risk.
